quick.summary: How to handle frustration when your model makes inevitable mistakes.
quick.takeaway: Compare your model to a smoke alarm to explain necessary trade offs.

beats.line: Sales got mad my model blocked a real buyer. How do I explain this?
Think of a smoke alarm in a busy kitchen.
It goes off when you burn toast.
Right. If you make it less sensitive, a real fire might spread.
Your model is a smoke alarm. It makes mistakes to keep you safe.
We measure this with a false positive rate.
Can I just say false alarms?
Yes. Explain the trade off using false alarms.
To stop all bad buyers, we get a few false alarms on good ones.
Perfect. Now they know what the system costs.

quiz.question: Your business partner is upset the model missed a fraud case. How do you respond?
options: It is like a smoke alarm. To avoid false alarms, it might miss a small fire.
The training data was biased against certain behaviors.
We can fix it by adding a billion more parameters.
The model is working perfectly and this is exactly as expected.
quiz.explanation: Comparing the model to an everyday object like a smoke alarm helps non-technical people grasp the trade offs of sensitivity.

quiz.question: You should hide the false positive rate so people trust the model more.
quiz.explanation: You should explain the cost of the model up front. Setting expectations builds trust when mistakes inevitably happen.
